messages.author: 54788cf3a8eb8916
messages.subject: Path Plot
parts:
Good morning from Dublin,

I would be interested in your feedback on some ggplot2 work I've been doing with an rstan fit object.  People kept saying to me that a sampler needs to explore the full space fairly thoroughly, so I tried to do a plot which would help to show this by plotting four sub-samples of 50 consecutive points (duplicates removed) from a given chain.  In the case of my simple  stan model, with only two parameters, it appears that 50 plot points is not really enough to explore the full region - but 50 is getting towards the limit of a visible path when plotted.  Refer attached pdf plot.

Refer to https://github.com/seanpor/RStanGraphics

For the purpose of demonstration I have put a fit object on github, and to use the function you just need to do something like...

source('stanGgplot.R')
# if you don't already have a fit object handy you could use this one
fit <- readRDS('sample_banana_fit_object.rds')
stanPathPlot(fit)

It is still early days on this, but I thought I'd share now.  Constructive feedback is most welcome.

Kind regards,

Sean O'Riordain
Trinity College,
Dublin
seor...@tcd.ie

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Path Plot
parts:
On 8/30/13 4:51 AM, Sean O'Riordain wrote:
> Good morning from Dublin,
>
> I would be interested in your feedback on some ggplot2 work I've been doing with an rstan fit object. People kept
> saying to me that a sampler needs to explore the full space fairly thoroughly,

Technically, it just needs to explore the space in proportion
to its posterior probability mass. For example, normal(0,1)
has support on (-inf,inf), but you're never going to see samples
outside of (-4,4) unless you do a whole lot of sampling.

How many samples you need practically depends on what you're
trying to estimate. If you're trying to estimate Pr(Y > 4)
accurately for some Y ~ normal(0,1), you're going to need a whole
lot more samples than if you're trying to estimate mean(Y) or
sd(Y).

> so I tried to do a plot which would help
> to show this by plotting four sub-samples of 50 consecutive points (duplicates removed) from a given chain. In the case
> of my simple stan model, with only two parameters, it appears that 50 plot points is not really enough to explore the
> full region - but 50 is getting towards the limit of a visible path when plotted. Refer attached pdf plot.
That looks pretty good for the banana distribution.

>
> Refer to https://github.com/seanpor/RStanGraphics
>
> For the purpose of demonstration I have put a fit object on github, and to use the function you just need to do
> something like...
>
> source('stanGgplot.R')
> # if you don't already have a fit object handy you could use this one
> fit <- readRDS('sample_banana_fit_object.rds')
> stanPathPlot(fit)
>
> It is still early days on this, but I thought I'd share now. Constructive feedback is most welcome.

You should take a look at Michael Betancourt's work on diagnostics in:

https://github.com/stan-dev/visual-diagnostics

If you could port some of Michael's diagnostics from gnuplot to ggplot2, it would
do all of us who use RStan a huge favor. The next release of Stan (2.0), should
also have a bit more built-in support for reporting diagnostic info like the
derivatives, which are very important for seeing what's going on with HMC (I'm not
positive about this, but Michael will know, since he wrote that, too). There's more
info in his arXiv papers with examples.

- Bob

On 8/31/13 2:44 AM, Sean O'Riordain wrote:
> Hi Bob,
>
> Thanks for your comments. Yes don't worry I had understood that it's in proportion to the posterior probability mass -
> but in the case of the above mentioned "banana" distribution", in some cases all four of the 50 sub-samples of the chain
> which has only 584 unique value pairs were all in the bottom "horizontal" part of the banana, which I felt was a bit
> "unlikely" :-)

I didn't see that in the plot --- it looked like you were getting both.

The banana's pretty tricky because there's no global
adaptation that Stan can do in terms of either a diagonal
or full mass matrix that makes sense because the correlation
structure is different in different parts of the banana. The best
you can do with Stan's current implementation is to find a small
enough scale that you can do a kind of random walk.

RMHMC does a much better job.

We should probably list this as one of our test examples since everybody
seems to like it.

> What I've been doing is running this plot a few times to see if the chains are getting "stuck".
>
> I will start on the translation of Michaels gnuplot code to ggplot2 on Monday morning first thing - shall I just put
> them in my github repository so you can take them from there?

That'll certainly work for now.

I think we'd eventually like to roll something like this into RStan
directly if you'd be willing to BSD license what you're doing.

The reason it's now standalone is that Michael's using gnuplot rather
than R, so it doesn't fit into RStan, and the GNU license is not
a dependency we want in the core Stan distribution.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Path Plot
parts:
Thanks!

I like the name:

# Simple Goel-Okumoto Non-Homogenous Poisson Process model

What we need to turn it into a test is actual posterior means
and variances for parameters we can test. So far we're not
testing covariance in the posterior. These can come from other software
or a really long run of Stan if you can verify it gets the right
answer.

Converting a Stan model to ana utomated model test requires
some work, so we're not going to get to it right
away. If you don't know C++ or googletest or don't want
to get into Daniels' model testing framework, it's probably
a lot easier if you let us do it.

- Bob

Hi Bob,
If you prefer to call it the real name... then the "banana" is fine with me :-)

I'm afraid my c++ is too weak even contemplate doing anything important like this! Feel free to do it - and ask any questions I could answer.  I'm not sure I follow you when you talk about turning it into a real test - perhaps you could elaborate please?

An alternate dataset is the "famous" NTDS published by Jelinski and Moranda in 1972 and heavily used in the discipline.... the published mode (by Goel and Okumoto 1979) is at the values alpha=33.99 and beta=0.00579 for the first 26 data points.

bugt <- c(9, 21, 32, 36, 43, 45, 50, 58, 63, 70, 71, 77,
  78, 87, 91, 92, 95, 98, 104, 105, 116, 149, 156, 247, 249, 250)
# restrict bugs to the first 26 elements to match the paper
# by Goel and Okumoto (1979)
N <- 26
bugs_dat <- list(N=N, bugs=bugt[1:N])

This looks less like a banana, and more like an L and requires about iter=120k and chains=4 to get n_eff approx 1000.

Currently working on Michael's plots...

cheers,
Seán

# by Goel and Okumoto (1979)

bugs_dat <- list(N=N, bugs=bugt[1:N])

Currently working on Michael's plots...

cheers,
Seán

Thanks!

I like the name:

# Simple Goel-Okumoto Non-Homogenous Poisson Process model

What we need to turn it into a test is actual posterior means
and variances for parameters we can test.   So far we're not
testing covariance in the posterior.  These can come from other software
or a really long run of Stan if you can verify it gets the right
answer.

Converting a Stan model to ana utomated model test requires
some work, so we're not going to get to it right
away.  If you don't know C++ or googletest or don't want
to get into Daniels' model testing framework, it's probably
a lot easier if you let us do it.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Path Plot
parts:
On 9/6/13 4:25 AM, Sean O'Riordain wrote:
> Hi Bob,

> If you prefer to call it the real name... then the "banana" is fine with me :-)
>
> I'm afraid my c++ is too weak even contemplate doing anything important like this! Feel free to do it - and ask any
> questions I could answer. I'm not sure I follow you when you talk about turning it into a real test - perhaps you could
> elaborate please?

We have model tests in C++ that run the models from various
starting points for a number of iterations and make sure the
posterior stats line up with what we expect --- primarily means
at this point, I think. We run them daily, and as new
patches are proposed, before we pull them, to make sure we
don't break model behavior during development.

I don't know that part of our code well, so I don't have
anything to say about configuring them.

We can add a test for this if we don't have it.

> An alternate dataset is the "famous" NTDS published by Jelinski and Moranda in 1972 and heavily used in the
> discipline.... the published mode (by Goel and Okumoto 1979) is at the values alpha=33.99 and beta=0.00579 for the first
> 26 data points.
>
> bugt <- c(9, 21, 32, 36, 43, 45, 50, 58, 63, 70, 71, 77,
> 78, 87, 91, 92, 95, 98, 104, 105, 116, 149, 156, 247, 249, 250)
> # restrict bugs to the first 26 elements to match the paper
> # by Goel and Okumoto (1979)
> N <- 26
> bugs_dat <- list(N=N, bugs=bugt[1:N])
>
> This looks less like a banana, and more like an L and requires about iter=120k and chains=4 to get n_eff approx 1000.

Ouch. RMHMC, which adapts to local curvature, will mix much
better on this (you can see examples of similar issues
solved in Michael Betancourt's arXiv papers on RMHMC).

- Bob
